title: Improving pyelonephritis on ceftriaxone; only oral beta-lactam options remain

clinical_review.notes: Case library v2 Batch A (#217): findings added from another module; awaiting owner review.

story: A 52-year-old woman with acute pyelonephritis is on IV ceftriaxone, hospital day 3. She has been afebrile for 36 hours, is eating and drinking, and her vital signs are normal. The urine E. coli is susceptible to ceftriaxone and to cefazolin at the urinary surrogate breakpoint, but resistant to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and ciprofloxacin. She has oxycodone 5 mg as needed for flank pain; no laxative is ordered.

prescriptions.instructions: 5 mg by mouth every 4 hours as needed for flank pain

cultures.order_text: Bacteria identified in Urine by Culture

expected_findings.summary: Clinical criteria for an oral switch are met; with the isolate susceptible to ceftriaxone, the oral option is a third-generation cephalosporin such as cefpodoxime.
Oxycodone as needed for flank pain with no stimulant or osmotic laxative ordered.

acceptable_answers: Switch to an oral third-generation cephalosporin (for example cefpodoxime), the isolate being ceftriaxone susceptible, as cefpodoxime 200 to 400 mg every 12 hours (IDSA 2025 Table 1.2; above the labeled dose, which covers uncomplicated UTI only), taken with food (antacids and H2 blockers reduce absorption), every 24 hours below a creatinine clearance of 30 mL/min and three times a week after hemodialysis, for a total course of about 7 days (IDSA 2025).
Continue IV ceftriaxone to complete a short course when oral therapy is not practical, documenting the reason.
Discuss with the team or infectious diseases before switching, given the very low certainty of the evidence for short non-fluoroquinolone courses.
reference_answer: Flag the patient as meeting clinical IV to PO criteria with an oral third-generation cephalosporin such as cefpodoxime, supported by the isolate's ceftriaxone susceptibility: IDSA 2025 calls this a reasonable switch after improvement on ceftriaxone, as cefpodoxime 200 to 400 mg every 12 hours (IDSA 2025 Table 1.2; above the labeled dose, which covers uncomplicated UTI only), taken with food (antacids and H2 blockers reduce absorption), every 24 hours below a creatinine clearance of 30 mL/min and three times a week after hemodialysis, for a total course of about 7 days. The finding should not present the switch as the only defensible choice. Add a bowel regimen with the oxycodone (senna or polyethylene glycol).
rationale: She meets clinical switch criteria, and the only susceptible oral agents are beta-lactams. The 2011 IDSA guideline considered oral beta-lactams less effective for pyelonephritis and advised a longer course; the 2025 IDSA complicated UTI guideline supersedes it: after improvement on ceftriaxone an oral third-generation cephalosporin is a reasonable switch, with optimized dosing and 7 days total for a non-fluoroquinolone (very low certainty), and no longer course for beta-lactams. Nitrofurantoin does not reach renal tissue. It stays an ambiguous case because the evidence for short oral beta-lactam courses is limited (owner review, 2026-11-12). Case library v2 (#217): adds the bowel regimen finding beside the ambiguous IV to PO question.

citations.supports: Switch to oral therapy once improving, able to take oral medication, with an effective oral option; after improvement on ceftriaxone an oral third-generation cephalosporin is a reasonable choice; checked against IDSA's published PDF and approved by the owner, 2026-11-12.

Oral agents for complicated UTI: oral third-generation cephalosporins may be comparable to fluoroquinolones or TMP-SMX; cephalexin, amoxicillin and low-bioavailability cephalosporins only with caution and optimized dosing; checked against IDSA's published PDF and approved by the owner, 2026-11-12.

7 days of a non-fluoroquinolone rather than 10-14 days; no longer course for oral beta-lactams, though higher doses may be required; checked against IDSA's published PDF and approved by the owner, 2026-11-12.
Cefpodoxime's labeled urinary use is uncomplicated UTI only; renal adjustment, food and acid suppression; checked against the DailyMed label and approved by the owner, 2026-11-12.

Enterobacterales breakpoints behind the panel. Its cefazolin urinary surrogate predicts oral cephalosporins only in uncomplicated UTI (E. coli, K. pneumoniae, P. mirabilis; Bryson et al., J Clin Microbiol 2024), so it is not the basis for step-down in pyelonephritis (owner, 2026-11-12).
Stewardship programs promoting timely IV to oral transition once criteria are met.
Statement 10: a bowel regimen with a stimulant or osmotic laxative for hospitalized patients on opioids unless contraindicated; owner approved 2026-11-16 (#202).
